Day 9 — Explainable AI
These are the exercises for one teaching day of Module 3 of the Health Data Science MSc. Each chapter is one exercise you can finish in a single sitting, with an R path and a Python path doing the same work. Pick one; in class we go through R most of the time.
Some tasks appear as code containing ______ for you to fill in. They are shown but not run, which is why no output appears beneath them. The worked answers are published after the session.

title: Exercise 9.1 — Variable importance, and a column of pure noise
text:
Day 5 ended with a random forest that predicts diabetes well but cannot be read like a tree or a logistic regression. The first question everyone asks of such a model is: which variables does it use? This exercise answers it in two ways, and then tests both with a column we know to be useless.






NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious, and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not expected to write it yourself.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger", "vip"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)                   # variable importance for many kinds of model

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables




Part 1 — The forest
The same 750 people and five predictors as Day 5, from data/diabetes_clean.csv: number of pregnancies, glucose, BMI (mass), the diabetes pedigree function and age. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

A random forest of 500 trees, as on Day 5. importance = "impurity" asks ranger to keep a record of how much each variable helped while it grows the trees; Part 2 reads it. A forest is random, so set the seed first.

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.753


The test AUC is 0.753. This is the model we explain all day. Python grows different random trees, so its numbers differ slightly.



Part 2 — Impurity importance
Impurity importance adds up, for each variable, how much purer its splits made the training rows, over all the trees. The forest works it out while it is fitted, so it is free. vi() from the vip package reads it. ranger reports a raw total; divide by the sum to get each variable’s share.

vi(rf_fit) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))

#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   Variable Importance share
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 glucose        80.2 0.373
#> 2 mass           39.2 0.182
#> 3 age            35.2 0.164
#> 4 pedigree       34.7 0.162
#> 5 pregnant       25.5 0.119


Glucose has 0.373 of the total, then BMI 0.182, age 0.164, pedigree 0.162 and pregnancies 0.119. Glucose comes first by a long way.



Part 3 — Permutation importance
Permutation importance asks a different question: how much worse is the model on the test rows if one variable is scrambled? Shuffle one column so its values land on the wrong people, predict again, and see how much the AUC drops. The model is not refitted.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
test_shuffled <- test |>
  mutate(glucose = sample(______))               # glucose now belongs to someone else

test_shuffled |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = ______, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")







TipStuck?





sample(glucose) returns the same glucose values in a random order. Then predict on the shuffled test rows, test_shuffled.



One shuffle is one random draw, so in Part 4 we repeat it 20 times for each variable and take the average drop.



Part 4 — A control: a column of pure noise
Which measure should we believe? Test both on something whose answer we already know: data/diabetes_noise.csv is the same file with one more column, noise: random numbers unrelated to anything. Its true importance is zero.
Read it, keep noise as a sixth predictor, and split it exactly as before. The same seed gives the same people in the test set.

diabetes_noise <- read_csv("data/diabetes_noise.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, noise, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split_noise <- initial_split(diabetes_noise, prop = 0.8)
train_noise <- training(split_noise)
test_noise  <- testing(split_noise)

Fit the same forest on these training rows and look at its impurity importance.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
rf_noise <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = ______)

vi(rf_noise) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))







TipStuck?





Use the training rows that contain the new column, train_noise. The formula diabetes ~ . picks up noise by itself.



Now the permutation importance of the same forest on the test rows. The loop does what you did in Part 3, 20 times for each of the six variables. Read it line by line; it takes a few seconds.

auc_before <- test_noise |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_noise, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
  pull(.estimate)

set.seed(1)
perm_results <- data.frame()                          # one row per shuffle

for (variable in c("pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "noise")) {
  for (repeat_number in 1:20) {
    test_shuffled <- test_noise
    test_shuffled[[variable]] <- sample(test_shuffled[[variable]])

    auc_after <- test_shuffled |>
      bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_shuffled, type = "prob")) |>
      roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
      pull(.estimate)

    perm_results <- bind_rows(perm_results,
                              data.frame(variable = variable,
                                         auc_drop = auc_before - auc_after))
  }
}

perm_importance <- perm_results |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(importance = mean(auc_drop), sd = sd(auc_drop)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

perm_importance

#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   variable importance      sd
#>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 glucose    0.129    0.0392 
#> 2 mass       0.0279   0.00840
#> 3 pedigree   0.0109   0.00899
#> 4 noise      0.000402 0.00898
#> 5 age       -0.00190  0.0134 
#> 6 pregnant  -0.00573  0.0147




Code for this plot (optional)
perm_importance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance, y = reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "coral") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = importance - sd, xmax = importance + sd),
                width = 0.3, orientation = "y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Mean drop in test AUC when the variable is shuffled (± 1 SD)",
       y = NULL, title = "Random forest: permutation importance")









noise comes out at 0.0004, with a standard deviation of 0.009: zero, as it should. Only glucose (0.129) and BMI (0.028) clearly beat it. The pedigree function (0.011) is within about one standard deviation of it, and age and pregnancies come out slightly below it: the forest predicts new people no better with them than without.
Why the difference? Deep trees always find some split on a column with many different values that tidies up a few training rows. Impurity importance counts that; permutation importance on new people does not. So a variable that does not clearly beat noise should not be called important.






TipKey points




Impurity importance is free and quick, but it is computed on the training rows and is biased: it gave pure noise 13% of the total.
Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one column is shuffled. Repeat the shuffle and report the mean and spread.
A noise column is a control: its true importance is zero, and permutation importance puts it there.






Download this exercise as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb): the text and every code cell of the Python version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Jupyter or VS Code and run it a cell at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance




Part 1 — The forest
The same 750 people and five predictors as Day 5, from data/diabetes_clean.csv: number of pregnancies, glucose, BMI (mass), the diabetes pedigree function and age. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

A random forest of 500 trees, as on Day 5. scikit-learn keeps a record of how much each variable helped while it grows the trees; Part 2 reads it. A forest is random, so fix random_state.

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

test_prob = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3)

#> 0.794


The test AUC is 0.794. This is the model we explain all day. R grows different random trees, so its numbers differ slightly.



Part 2 — Impurity importance
Impurity importance adds up, for each variable, how much purer its splits made the training rows, over all the trees. The forest works it out while it is fitted, so it is free. scikit-learn stores it in feature_importances_, one number per predictor, already scaled to add up to 1.

impurity_importance = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=predictors)
impurity_importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)

#> glucose     0.318
#> mass        0.205
#> pedigree    0.198
#> age         0.169
#> pregnant    0.109
#> dtype: float64


Glucose has 0.318 of the total, then BMI 0.205, pedigree 0.198, age 0.169 and pregnancies 0.109. Glucose comes first by a long way.



Part 3 — Permutation importance
Permutation importance asks a different question: how much worse is the model on the test rows if one variable is scrambled? Shuffle one column so its values land on the wrong people, predict again, and see how much the AUC drops. The model is not refitted.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
test_shuffled = test.copy()
test_shuffled["glucose"] = rng.permutation(test_shuffled[______].values)   # glucose now belongs to someone else

shuffled_prob = rf.predict_proba(______[predictors])[:, 1]
round(roc_auc_score(test_shuffled["diabetes"], shuffled_prob), 3)







TipStuck?





rng.permutation() returns the same glucose values in a random order. Then predict on the shuffled test rows, test_shuffled.



One shuffle is one random draw, so in Part 4 we repeat it 20 times for each variable and take the average drop.



Part 4 — A control: a column of pure noise
Which measure should we believe? Test both on something whose answer we already know: data/diabetes_noise.csv is the same file with one more column, noise: random numbers unrelated to anything. Its true importance is zero.
Read it, keep noise as a sixth predictor, and split it exactly as before. The same random_state gives the same people in the test set.

diabetes_noise = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_noise.csv")
diabetes_noise["diabetes"] = (diabetes_noise["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)

predictors_noise = predictors + ["noise"]

train_noise, test_noise = train_test_split(diabetes_noise, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

Fit the same forest on these training rows and look at its impurity importance.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rf_noise = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf_noise = rf_noise.fit(train_noise[______], train_noise["diabetes"])

pd.Series(rf_noise.feature_importances_, index=predictors_noise).sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)







TipStuck?





The forest now uses all six predictors, predictors_noise.



Now the permutation importance of the same forest on the test rows. permutation_importance() does what you did in Part 3, 20 times for each of the six variables, with scoring="roc_auc".

perm = permutation_importance(rf_noise, test_noise[predictors_noise],
                              test_noise["diabetes"], scoring="roc_auc",
                              n_repeats=20, random_state=1)

perm_importance = pd.DataFrame({"variable": predictors_noise,
                                "importance": perm.importances_mean,
                                "sd": perm.importances_std})
perm_importance = perm_importance.sort_values("importance", ascending=False)
perm_importance.round(3)

#>    variable  importance     sd
#> 1   glucose       0.150  0.041
#> 2      mass       0.031  0.019
#> 4       age       0.029  0.016
#> 0  pregnant       0.012  0.021
#> 3  pedigree       0.006  0.008
#> 5     noise      -0.005  0.008




Code for this plot (optional)
ordered = perm_importance.sort_values("importance")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(ordered["variable"], ordered["importance"], xerr=ordered["sd"],
        color="coral", capsize=3)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean drop in test AUC when the variable is shuffled (± 1 SD)")
ax.set_title("Random forest: permutation importance")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()









noise comes out at −0.005, with a standard deviation of 0.008: zero, as it should. Glucose (0.150), BMI (0.031) and age (0.029) clearly beat it. Pregnancies (0.012) and the pedigree function (0.006) are within about one standard deviation of it.
Why the difference? Deep trees always find some split on a column with many different values that tidies up a few training rows. Impurity importance counts that; permutation importance on new people does not. So a variable that does not clearly beat noise should not be called important.






TipKey points




Impurity importance is free and quick, but it is computed on the training rows and is biased: it gave pure noise 15% of the total.
Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one column is shuffled. Repeat the shuffle and report the mean and spread.
A noise column is a control: its true importance is zero, and permutation importance puts it there.

title: Exercise 9.2 — SHAP values: global and local explanations
text:
Exercise 9.1 ranked the variables for the forest as a whole. It did not say which way a variable pushes the risk, and it said nothing about any one patient. SHAP values do both. For every patient and every variable, a SHAP value says how much that variable moved this patient’s predicted probability away from the average prediction.
Goal. In this exercise you will:

compute SHAP values for the test patients and check that they add up to the prediction;
read two global plots: the mean absolute SHAP bar plot and the beeswarm;
read the waterfall plot for one patient.







NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious, and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not expected to write it yourself.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger", "kernelshap", "shapviz"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(kernelshap)            # computes SHAP values for any model
library(shapviz)               # plots SHAP values

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables

The same data (data/diabetes_clean.csv), outcome and five predictors as Exercise 9.1.

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

The same random forest as Exercise 9.1, fitted on the training rows and evaluated once on the test rows.

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.753


The forest reaches a test AUC of 0.753.



Part 1 — SHAP values for the test patients
Start from the baseline: the average prediction. A patient’s SHAP values share out the gap between the baseline and that patient’s prediction, one piece per variable. A positive value pushes the risk up; a negative value pushes it down. Added together, they give the prediction exactly:
baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction.
kernelshap computes SHAP values for any model. A variable we “do not know” is filled in from a background sample of 100 training patients. We explain the 150 test patients, and shapviz keeps the values for the probability of pos. This takes about 15 seconds.

set.seed(1)
background <- train |>
  slice_sample(n = 100) |>
  select(-diabetes)

shap_rf <- kernelshap(rf_fit, X = test |> select(-diabetes), bg_X = background,
                      type = "prob", verbose = FALSE)

sv_pos <- shapviz(shap_rf)$.pred_pos       # SHAP values for the probability of pos

dim(get_shap_values(sv_pos))               # one row per patient, one column per predictor

#> [1] 150   5

get_baseline(sv_pos)                       # the average prediction

#> [1] 0.364168


The baseline is 0.364. Now check that it adds up for the first test patient.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient_shap <- get_shap_values(sv_pos)[1, ]
patient_shap

get_baseline(sv_pos) + ______(patient_shap)
test_preds$.pred_pos[1]







TipStuck?





You want to add up the five SHAP values in patient_shap. The R function that adds up a vector is sum().






Part 2 — The global view: bar plot and beeswarm
We now have 150 × 5 SHAP values. The mean absolute SHAP value of a variable says how far, on average, it moves a patient’s prediction, up or down. It is a variable importance, in units of probability.

get_shap_values(sv_pos) |>
  abs() |>
  colMeans() |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)

#>    glucose       mass        age   pregnant   pedigree 
#> 0.16201681 0.06579994 0.05498385 0.04724774 0.02651746


Glucose moves a prediction by 0.162 on average. The other four variables move it by between 0.027 and 0.066.
The bar plot draws the same numbers:


Code for this plot (optional)
sv_importance(sv_pos, fill = "steelblue")









The beeswarm shows every patient. Each dot is one patient’s SHAP value for one variable. The colour is the patient’s value of that variable, from low to high.


Code for this plot (optional)
sv_importance(sv_pos, kind = "beeswarm")









Question! In the glucose row, where are the patients with high glucose, and where are those with low glucose?
High glucose sits on the right: it pushes the risk up, by as much as 0.424. Low glucose sits on the left and pushes it down, by as much as 0.362. The bar plot gives only the size of each effect. The beeswarm also gives its direction, patient by patient.



Part 3 — One patient: the waterfall plot
A local explanation answers: why did the model give this patient this risk? Take the first test patient again:

test_preds |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes, .pred_pos)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   pregnant glucose  mass pedigree   age diabetes .pred_pos
#>      <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <fct>        <dbl>
#> 1        0     194  28.5     0.24    28 neg          0.706


She is 28, with no pregnancies, a BMI of 28.5 and a glucose of 194 mg/dL, and she does not have diabetes. The waterfall plot starts at the baseline at the bottom and adds one SHAP value at a time, up to her prediction at the top.


Code for this plot (optional)
sv_waterfall(sv_pos, row_id = 1)









Read in words: the average patient has a predicted risk of 0.364. Her very high glucose adds 0.353. Her other values change it by 0.035 or less. Her predicted risk is 0.706, so at a threshold of 0.5 she is a false positive. The explanation tells us what the model did, not whether it was right.
Your turn. Draw the waterfall for the test patient the model thinks is at highest risk.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
highest <- which.max(test_preds$______)     # the row number of the highest probability
test_preds |> slice(highest)

sv_waterfall(sv_pos, row_id = ______)







TipStuck?





which.max() returns the position of the largest value in a vector. The vector you want is the predicted probability of pos. Then pass that position as row_id.









TipKey points




A SHAP value is one variable’s push on one patient’s prediction, up or down from the baseline (the average prediction).
Baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction, exactly.
Mean absolute SHAP ranks the variables; the beeswarm also shows the direction of each effect.
The waterfall plot explains one patient’s prediction. It says what the model did, not whether the model was right.






Download this exercise as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb): the text and every code cell of the Python version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Jupyter or VS Code and run it a cell at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn shap

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import shap

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

The same data (data/diabetes_clean.csv), outcome and five predictors as Exercise 9.1.

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

The same random forest as Exercise 9.1, fitted on the training rows and evaluated once on the test rows.

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

test_prob = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

print("test AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3))

#> test AUC: 0.794


The forest reaches a test AUC of 0.794.



Part 1 — SHAP values for the test patients
Start from the baseline: the average prediction. A patient’s SHAP values share out the gap between the baseline and that patient’s prediction, one piece per variable. A positive value pushes the risk up; a negative value pushes it down. Added together, they give the prediction exactly:
baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction.
The shap package’s TreeExplainer uses the structure of the trees to compute exact SHAP values in under a second. We explain the 150 test patients and keep the values for class 1, diabetes.

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)
explanation = explainer(test[predictors])

shap_pos = explanation[:, :, 1]            # SHAP values for class 1 (diabetes)

print("shape:   ", shap_pos.values.shape)  # one row per patient, one column per predictor

#> shape:    (150, 5)

print("baseline:", round(shap_pos.base_values[0], 3))   # the average prediction

#> baseline: 0.359


The baseline is 0.359. Now check that it adds up for the first test patient.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient_shap = shap_pos.values[0]
print(np.round(patient_shap, 3))

print(shap_pos.base_values[0] + patient_shap.______())
print(test_prob[0])







TipStuck?





You want to add up the five SHAP values in patient_shap. NumPy arrays have a .sum() method.






Part 2 — The global view: bar plot and beeswarm
We now have 150 × 5 SHAP values. The mean absolute SHAP value of a variable says how far, on average, it moves a patient’s prediction, up or down. It is a variable importance, in units of probability.

shap_importance = pd.Series(np.abs(shap_pos.values).mean(axis=0), index=predictors)

shap_importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)

#> glucose     0.159
#> age         0.066
#> mass        0.060
#> pregnant    0.049
#> pedigree    0.034
#> dtype: float64


Glucose moves a prediction by 0.159 on average. The other four variables move it by between 0.034 and 0.066.
The bar plot draws the same numbers:


Code for this plot (optional)
shap.plots.bar(shap_pos, show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The beeswarm shows every patient. Each dot is one patient’s SHAP value for one variable. The colour is the patient’s value of that variable, blue low and red high.


Code for this plot (optional)
shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_pos, show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Question! In the glucose row, where are the patients with high glucose, and where are those with low glucose?
High glucose sits on the right: it pushes the risk up, by as much as 0.480. Low glucose sits on the left and pushes it down, by as much as 0.313. The bar plot gives only the size of each effect. The beeswarm also gives its direction, patient by patient.



Part 3 — One patient: the waterfall plot
A local explanation answers: why did the model give this patient this risk? Take the first test patient again:

patient = test.iloc[[0]]                   # double brackets keep it a one-row table
print(patient)

#>      pregnant  glucose  mass  pedigree  age  diabetes
#> 506         6      115  28.8     0.368   35         0

print("predicted probability:", round(test_prob[0], 3))

#> predicted probability: 0.276


She is 35, with 6 pregnancies, a BMI of 28.8 and a glucose of 115 mg/dL, and she does not have diabetes. The waterfall plot starts at the baseline at the bottom and adds one SHAP value at a time, up to her prediction at the top.


Code for this plot (optional)
shap.plots.waterfall(shap_pos[0], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Read in words: the average patient has a predicted risk of 0.359. Her ordinary glucose takes 0.139 off. Her age, BMI and pregnancies each add a little (0.032 or less), and her pedigree function takes off 0.021. Her predicted risk is 0.276: below 0.5, so she is correctly predicted as neg.
Your turn. Draw the waterfall for the test patient the model thinks is at highest risk.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
highest = test_prob.______()                # the position of the highest probability
print(test.iloc[[highest]])

shap.plots.waterfall(shap_pos[______], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







TipStuck?





NumPy arrays have .argmax(), the position of the largest value. Then use that position to pick the patient out of shap_pos.









TipKey points




A SHAP value is one variable’s push on one patient’s prediction, up or down from the baseline (the average prediction).
Baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction, exactly.
Mean absolute SHAP ranks the variables; the beeswarm also shows the direction of each effect.
The waterfall plot explains one patient’s prediction. It says what the model did, not whether the model was right.

title: Exercise 9.3 — One toolbox for explanations: DALEX
text:
Exercises 9.1 and 9.2 used a different package for each explanation. The DALEX package puts them behind one interface. You wrap the fitted model once in an explainer, then ask the explainer each question. The package exists in R (with DALEXtra for tidymodels) and in Python (dalex), with the same function names.






NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious, and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not expected to write it yourself.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "DALEX", "DALEXtra", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX)                 # explanations for any model
library(DALEXtra)              # connects DALEX to tidymodels

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables

The data are the 750 people in data/diabetes_clean.csv, as in Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. The outcome is diabetes (neg or pos); the predictors are pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree and age, in their own units. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)




Part 1 — The model and the explainer
The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. Fit it on the training rows:

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

Evaluate it once on the test set:

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

test_preds |> accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric  .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 accuracy binary          0.72

test_preds |> roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.753


Accuracy 0.720 and AUC 0.753 on the 150 test patients.
Now wrap the model in an explainer. explain_tidymodels() needs the model, the predictors of the people to explain it on (the test patients), and the true outcome y as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = test |> select(-diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == ______),   # 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
  label = "Random forest",
  verbose = FALSE                                # no progress report
)







TipStuck?





y must be 1 for the people with diabetes. Which level of diabetes is that? as.numeric(test$diabetes) on its own would give 1 and 2 (the positions of the levels), and every explanation would then be wrong.



A quick check that the explainer is set up right: its AUC should be the one you just computed.

model_performance(explainer)$measures |> as.data.frame()

#>      recall precision        f1 accuracy       auc
#> 1 0.6181818 0.6181818 0.6181818     0.72 0.7525359


It is, 0.753.



Part 2 — Which variables matter?
model_parts() is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: shuffle one variable in the test set, see how much worse the model gets, repeat 10 times and average. DALEX measures “worse” as \(1 - \text{AUC}\), so a larger number is a worse model. _full_model_ is the value with nothing shuffled.

set.seed(1)
importance_dalex <- model_parts(explainer)

importance_dalex |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(permutation == 0) |>        # permutation 0 is the average of the 10 shuffles
  select(variable, dropout_loss)

#>       variable dropout_loss
#> 1 _full_model_    0.2474641
#> 2     pregnant    0.2481148
#> 3          age    0.2547177
#> 4     pedigree    0.2586411
#> 5         mass    0.2800574
#> 6      glucose    0.3796555
#> 7   _baseline_    0.4769761


With nothing shuffled the loss is 0.247. Shuffling glucose raises it to 0.380; shuffling any other variable raises it by 0.033 at most (BMI). Glucose is by far the most important variable, as in Exercise 9.1, and here it took one line of code.



Part 3 — How does the prediction change with glucose?
An importance says how much a variable matters, not how. For one patient, set her glucose to 57, then a little higher, and so on up to 194, keep everything else about her as it is, and predict each time. The curve you get is her ICE profile (individual conditional expectation). The average of the 150 ICE profiles is the partial dependence profile: what the model predicts, on average, at each glucose level. model_profile() computes both.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_glucose <- model_profile(explainer, variables = ______, type = "partial",
                             N = NULL,                         # use all 150 patients
                             variable_splits_type = "uniform") # an evenly spaced grid







TipStuck?





Give the name of the variable as a string, in quotes.





Code for this plot (optional)
pdp_glucose$cp_profiles |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = glucose, y = `_yhat_`, group = `_ids_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_glucose$agr_profiles,
            aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`, group = NULL),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes",
       title = "ICE profiles (grey) and partial dependence (blue)")









Question! Describe the blue curve in words. Do all the grey curves have the same shape?
Below a glucose of about 100 the average prediction stays low, between 0.14 and 0.24. It climbs gradually to about 0.40 at 140, rises steeply between 145 and 157 to about 0.68, and stays between 0.66 and 0.73 above that. The steps come from the forest’s splits. Every grey curve ends higher than it starts, but they start at different heights (from 0.07 to 0.47) and rise by very different amounts (from 0.15 to 0.75). How much glucose matters depends on a patient’s other values; the average curve hides that.



Part 4 — One patient
predict_parts() explains one prediction. Take the first test patient:

new_observation <- test |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(-diabetes)

new_observation

#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   pregnant glucose  mass pedigree   age
#>      <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1        0     194  28.5     0.24    28

predict(explainer, new_observation)          # her predicted probability

#>       pos 
#> 0.7058381


Ask for her SHAP values, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates them from 25 random orders of the variables, with the test patients as the background.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
shap_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                              type = ______, B = 25)

shap_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(B == 0) |>                    # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
  select(variable, contribution) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))







TipStuck?





The type is a string, the name of the method in lower case. See ?predict_parts.



She is 28, with a glucose of 194, and the forest gives her 0.706. The average prediction over the test patients is 0.379. Her glucose adds +0.361; each of the other four variables moves it by 0.04 or less. As in Exercise 9.2, the contributions add up from the average to her prediction. With type = "break_down" DALEX adds the variables in one fixed order instead of averaging over many.






TipKey points




Wrap the fitted model once in an explainer, with the test patients and y coded 1 for diabetes and 0 for none. Every explanation is then one function call.
model_parts() is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: glucose matters most.
model_profile() gives the partial dependence profile (the average) and the ICE profiles (one per patient) for one variable. Read both: the average can hide patients who differ.
predict_parts() explains one patient, with SHAP values as in Exercise 9.2.






Download this exercise as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb): the text and every code cell of the Python version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Jupyter or VS Code and run it a cell at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn "dalex>=1.8"

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import dalex as dx             # explanations for any model

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score

The data are the 750 people in data/diabetes_clean.csv, as in Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. The outcome is diabetes, coded 1 for pos and 0 for neg; the predictors are pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree and age, in their own units. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)




Part 1 — The model and the explainer
The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. Fit it on the training rows:

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

Evaluate it once on the test set:

test_class = rf.predict(test[predictors])                # predicted class, threshold 0.5
test_prob  = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

print("accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))

#> accuracy: 0.713

print("AUC:     ", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3))

#> AUC:      0.794


Accuracy 0.713 and AUC 0.794 on the 150 test patients.
Now wrap the model in an explainer. dx.Explainer() needs the model, the predictors of the people to explain it on (the test patients), and the true outcome y as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer = dx.Explainer(
    rf,
    data=test[______],
    y=test["diabetes"],                           # already 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
    label="Random forest",
    verbose=False,                                # no progress report
)







TipStuck?





data is the table of predictors only, without the outcome column: the same columns the forest was fitted on.



A quick check that the explainer is set up right: its AUC should be the one you just computed.

explainer.model_performance().result.round(3)

#>                recall  precision     f1  accuracy    auc
#> Random forest   0.474      0.675  0.557     0.713  0.794


It is, 0.794.



Part 2 — Which variables matter?
model_parts() is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: shuffle one variable in the test set, see how much worse the model gets, repeat 10 times and average. DALEX measures “worse” as \(1 - \text{AUC}\), so a larger number is a worse model. _full_model_ is the value with nothing shuffled.

importance_dalex = explainer.model_parts(random_state=1)

importance_dalex.result[["variable", "dropout_loss"]].round(3)

#>        variable  dropout_loss
#> 0      pedigree         0.205
#> 1  _full_model_         0.206
#> 2      pregnant         0.218
#> 3          mass         0.234
#> 4           age         0.242
#> 5       glucose         0.352
#> 6    _baseline_         0.517


With nothing shuffled the loss is 0.206. Shuffling glucose raises it to 0.352; shuffling any other variable raises it by 0.036 at most (age), and shuffling pedigree changes it by less than 0.001. Glucose is by far the most important variable, as in Exercise 9.1, and here it took one line of code.



Part 3 — How does the prediction change with glucose?
An importance says how much a variable matters, not how. For one patient, set her glucose to 73, then a little higher, and so on up to 196, keep everything else about her as it is, and predict each time. The curve you get is her ICE profile (individual conditional expectation). The average of the 150 ICE profiles is the partial dependence profile: what the model predicts, on average, at each glucose level. model_profile() computes both.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_glucose = explainer.model_profile(variables=[______], type="partial",
                                      verbose=False)







TipStuck?





Give the name of the variable as a string, in quotes, inside the list.





Code for this plot (optional)
ice = pdp_glucose.raw_profiles.result

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for patient_id in ice["_ids_"].unique():
    one = ice[ice["_ids_"] == patient_id]
    ax.plot(one["glucose"], one["_yhat_"], color="grey", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(pdp_glucose.result["_x_"], pdp_glucose.result["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted probability of diabetes")
ax.set_title("ICE profiles (grey) and partial dependence (blue)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Question! Describe the blue curve in words. Do all the grey curves have the same shape?
Below a glucose of about 100 the average prediction stays low, between 0.15 and 0.20. It climbs gradually to about 0.37 at 140, rises steeply between 145 and 157 to about 0.66, and stays between 0.63 and 0.67 above that. The steps come from the forest’s splits. Every grey curve ends higher than it starts, but they start at different heights (from 0.04 to 0.64) and rise by very different amounts (from 0.08 to 0.85). How much glucose matters depends on a patient’s other values; the average curve hides that.



Part 4 — One patient
predict_parts() explains one prediction. Take the first test patient:

new_observation = test[predictors].iloc[[0]]

print(new_observation)

#>      pregnant  glucose  mass  pedigree  age
#> 506         6      115  28.8     0.368   35

print(explainer.predict(new_observation))     # her predicted probability

#> [0.276]


Ask for her SHAP values, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates them from 25 random orders of the variables, with the test patients as the background.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
shap_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type=______, B=25,
                                       random_state=1)

shap_average = shap_patient.result[shap_patient.result["B"] == 0]   # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
shap_average = shap_average[["variable", "contribution"]]
shap_average.sort_values("contribution", key=abs, ascending=False).round(3)







TipStuck?





The type is a string, the name of the method in lower case. See help(explainer.predict_parts).



This split puts a different person first than the R split does. She is 35, with a glucose of 115, and the forest gives her 0.276. The average prediction over the test patients is 0.356. Her glucose pulls the prediction down by 0.144; each of the other four variables moves it by 0.036 or less. As in Exercise 9.2, the contributions add up from the average to her prediction. With type="break_down" DALEX adds the variables in one fixed order instead of averaging over many.






TipKey points




Wrap the fitted model once in an explainer, with the test patients and y coded 1 for diabetes and 0 for none. Every explanation is then one function call.
model_parts() is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: glucose matters most.
model_profile() gives the partial dependence profile (the average) and the ICE profiles (one per patient) for one variable. Read both: the average can hide patients who differ.
predict_parts() explains one patient, with SHAP values as in Exercise 9.2.

title: Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
text:
ImportantA suggested addition, not part of the original module



This exercise has no page in the original version of the module. Exercises 9.1 to 9.3 explain the model as a whole and one patient at a time; this one asks whether it works equally well for different groups of patients. Accept, rewrite or remove it; nothing else depends on it.


One test AUC describes the model for all the test patients together. The model can still serve some groups much worse than others, and the overall number will not show it. Here we split the test patients by age and by BMI and compare.






NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious, and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not expected to write it yourself.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

The model

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables

The same data (data/diabetes_clean.csv) and random forest as Exercises 9.1 to 9.3. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

Evaluate it once on all the test rows (threshold 0.5):

class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, sens)
class_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   .metric  .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 accuracy binary         0.72 
#> 2 sens     binary         0.618

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 roc_auc binary         0.753


Accuracy 0.720, sensitivity 0.618, AUC 0.753. These are the overall numbers we will now break down.



Part 1 — Performance by age group
Put the test patients into three age groups. For each group, count the patients, the patients with diabetes and how many of those the model catches, then work out the accuracy and the sensitivity.

test_preds <- test_preds |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(20, 29, 39, Inf),
                         labels = c("21-29", "30-39", "40 and over")))

test_preds |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            with_diabetes = sum(diabetes == "pos"),
            caught = sum(diabetes == "pos" & .pred_class == "pos"),
            accuracy = mean(.pred_class == diabetes),
            sensitivity = caught / with_diabetes)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   age_group   patients with_diabetes caught accuracy sensitivity
#>   <fct>          <int>         <int>  <int>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 21-29             84            24      9    0.75        0.375
#> 2 30-39             32            12     10    0.781       0.833
#> 3 40 and over       34            19     15    0.588       0.789


yardstick’s functions also work on grouped data, one row per group. The AUC for each age group:

test_preds |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")

#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   age_group   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <fct>       <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 21-29       roc_auc binary         0.737
#> 2 30-39       roc_auc binary         0.8  
#> 3 40 and over roc_auc binary         0.558


Question! Which age group does the model serve worst?
It depends on the measure. In the youngest group the accuracy looks fine (0.750), but the model catches only 9 of the 24 people with diabetes (sensitivity 0.375); most young people do not have diabetes, so being right about them keeps the accuracy up. In the oldest group it catches 15 of 19, but it has the lowest accuracy (0.588) and an AUC of 0.558, close to the 0.5 of a coin toss. None of this shows in the overall numbers.
The plot shows the predicted probabilities in each age group, split by whether the patient really has diabetes. Most of the young people with diabetes sit below the 0.5 line.


Code for this plot (optional)
test_preds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = .pred_pos, colour = diabetes)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, seed = 1), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes", colour = "Diabetes")












Part 2 — By BMI, and how far to trust a small group
Your turn. Do the same with two BMI groups: under 30, and 30 or over (the usual cut-off for obesity).

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
test_preds <- test_preds |>
  mutate(bmi_group = if_else(mass < ______, "under 30", "30 and over"))

test_preds |>
  group_by(bmi_group) |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            with_diabetes = sum(diabetes == "pos"),
            caught = sum(diabetes == "pos" & .pred_class == "pos"),
            accuracy = mean(.pred_class == diabetes),
            sensitivity = caught / with_diabetes)

test_preds |>
  group_by(______) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")







TipStuck?





BMI is the column mass, and the cut-off is 30. Group by the new column, bmi_group.



How far can we trust these numbers? The sensitivity of 0.364 in the BMI-under-30 group rests on 11 people: 4 caught out of 11. One more caught would make it 0.455, one fewer 0.273. With so few people, one patient moves the number a long way, and a different random split could tell a different story. Differences between small groups are a reason to look again with more data, not a finding. That is why the counts always go beside the metrics.






TipKey points

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score

The same data (data/diabetes_clean.csv) and random forest as Exercises 9.1 to 9.3. As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

test_preds = test.copy()
test_preds["prob"] = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]   # probability of diabetes
test_preds["pred"] = rf.predict(test[predictors])               # predicted class, threshold 0.5

Evaluate it once on all the test rows (threshold 0.5):

print("accuracy   ", round(accuracy_score(test_preds["diabetes"], test_preds["pred"]), 3))

#> accuracy    0.713

print("sensitivity", round(recall_score(test_preds["diabetes"], test_preds["pred"]), 3))

#> sensitivity 0.474

print("AUC        ", round(roc_auc_score(test_preds["diabetes"], test_preds["prob"]), 3))

#> AUC         0.794


Accuracy 0.713, sensitivity 0.474, AUC 0.794. These are the overall numbers we will now break down.



Part 1 — Performance by age group
Put the test patients into three age groups. The loop takes one group at a time and records the number of patients, the patients with diabetes, how many of those the model catches, the accuracy, the sensitivity and the AUC.

test_preds["age_group"] = pd.cut(test_preds["age"], bins=[20, 29, 39, np.inf],
                                 labels=["21-29", "30-39", "40 and over"])

rows = []
for group, patients in test_preds.groupby("age_group", observed=True):
    rows.append({"age_group": group,
                 "patients": len(patients),
                 "with_diabetes": patients["diabetes"].sum(),
                 "caught": ((patients["diabetes"] == 1) & (patients["pred"] == 1)).sum(),
                 "accuracy": accuracy_score(patients["diabetes"], patients["pred"]),
                 "sensitivity": recall_score(patients["diabetes"], patients["pred"]),
                 "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(patients["diabetes"], patients["prob"])})

pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)

#>      age_group  patients  with_diabetes  caught  accuracy  sensitivity  roc_auc
#> 0        21-29        89             26      10     0.775        0.385    0.803
#> 1        30-39        25             11       8     0.720        0.727    0.818
#> 2  40 and over        36             20       9     0.556        0.450    0.669


Question! Which age group does the model serve worst?
It depends on the measure. In the youngest group the accuracy looks fine (0.775), but the model catches only 10 of the 26 people with diabetes (sensitivity 0.385); most young people do not have diabetes, so being right about them keeps the accuracy up. The oldest group has the lowest accuracy (0.556) and the lowest AUC (0.669), and the model catches only 9 of its 20 cases. None of this shows in the overall numbers.
The plot shows the predicted probabilities in each age group, split by whether the patient really has diabetes. Most of the young people with diabetes sit below the 0.5 line.


Code for this plot (optional)
groups = ["21-29", "30-39", "40 and over"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
for shift, outcome, colour in [(-0.2, 0, "tab:blue"), (0.2, 1, "tab:red")]:
    for i, group in enumerate(groups):
        values = test_preds.loc[(test_preds["age_group"] == group) &
                                (test_preds["diabetes"] == outcome), "prob"]
        ax.boxplot(values, positions=[i + shift], widths=0.3, showfliers=False)
        ax.scatter(np.full(len(values), i + shift), values, color=colour, alpha=0.5,
                   label=("diabetes" if outcome == 1 else "no diabetes") if i == 0 else None)
ax.axhline(0.5, color="black", linestyle="--")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(groups)))
ax.set_xticklabels(groups)
ax.set_xlabel("Age group")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted probability of diabetes")
ax.legend(title="Diabetes", loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

How far can we trust these numbers? The sensitivity of 0.083 in the BMI-under-30 group rests on 12 people: 1 caught out of 12. One more caught would double it to 0.167. With so few people, one patient moves the number a long way, and a different random split could tell a different story.
